newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan conservative parties flirt with grand union.
newsitem.headline: Japan conservative parties flirt with grand union.

text.p: A handshake last week between the prime minister and opposition leader, which assured the future of U.S. bases in Japan, has stirred speculation of a wider embrace between the country's two biggest political parties.

Talk of a coalition between Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) and Ichiro Ozawa's Shinshinto (New Frontier Party) has surfaced time and again ever since the opposition party was formed in late 1994.

But schemes to unite the two conservative groups -- a dream of LDP elders who pine for the 1955-93 era when the party dominated parliament and didn't have to cater to coalition parties -- have foundered on bitter personal rivalries.

However, an April 3 agreement between Hashimoto and Ozawa to push through legislation to override the refusal of Okinawan landowners to lease land for U.S. bases marked the first time the two big parties have cooperated on a major policy issue.

Political analysts have new grist for a "grand union" theory in an Ozawa interview in next month's issue of the influential monthly opinion journal Bungei Shunju, excerpts of which appeared in newspapers on Tuesday.

In the interview, to appear on newsstands on Thursday, Ozawa mixes swipes at the LDP's awkward three-year-old coalition with former Cold War foe, the left-leaning Social Democratic Party, with thinly-veiled appeals to the Liberal Democrats.

"As domestic and external problems become more serious, I expect that members of the LDP will increasingly debate whether (the alliance of convenience with the Socialists) is a good thing or a bad thing," Ozawa says.
"In the end, it comes down to individual lawmakers' ideology, ideals and philosophy," the Shinshinto head said.

The LDP, which in October general elections came a dozen seats shy of a working majority in the 500-seat Lower House of parliament, has relied on the Socialists' 15 seats to pass the state budget and other legislation.
Working with the Social Democrats, however, has been frustrating and time-consuming for the LDP -- especially on defence and foreign policy issues.
Ozawa, who almost single-handedly ended the LDP's long rule when he split the party in 1993, has himself tried and been unable to form a lasting coalition with the Social Democrats.

His calls for a union with LDP members who share his vision of a Japan with a deregulated economy, small government and more assertive defence and foreign policies have often been shrugged off as a ploy to split the ruling party again.

Although many LDP members resent Ozawa for his defection and what they say is his high-handedness, his policy appeal resonates with influential party elders, who want to restore robust leadership to Japan after years of drift.

Former Prime Minister Yasuhiro Nakasone, who headed Japan from 1982-87 and was arguably Tokyo's last strong leader, on Monday called for a "grand deregulation alliance" in a speech many analysts read as a new appeal to Shinshinto.
But not so fast, says LDP Secretary-General Koichi Kato, the party's second-ranking leader after Hashimoto and a staunch critic of Ozawa and his policies.

Kato, seen as a leading proponent of maintaining the LDP's coalition with the Social Democrats and the tiny liberal group Sakigake and keeping Ozawa's team out of power, says the Okinawa deal was a one-off deal overblown by Japan's media.

In an interview with the leading business daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun, Kato said the LDP would likely continue policy talks with other parties, including Shinshinto, but that Ozawa's party would be "the hardest to join forces with".
"The LDP and Shinshinto are in life-or-death election fights in about 271 of the 300 first-past-the-post constituencies," said Kato.
"Most of the LDP's proponents of the conservative coalition are those who don't have to worry about a clash with Shinshinto candidates."
